questions.stem: Which three levels make up biodiversity?
options: Kingdom, phylum and class diversity
Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity
Cell, tissue and organ diversity
Producer, consumer and decomposer diversity
questions.explanation: Biodiversity includes the variety of genes within species, the variety of species, and the variety of ecosystems. Producers, consumers and decomposers are trophic roles, not levels of biodiversity.

questions.stem: Which example describes genetic diversity?
options: The total mass of plant material produced in a woodland
Differences in alleles among the jarrah trees of one forest
The number of different bird species found in a wetland
The range of reefs, mangroves and seagrass beds in a bay
questions.explanation: Genetic diversity is the variety of alleles within a species or population. A count of species is species diversity, and a range of habitats is ecosystem diversity.

questions.stem: What does the species richness of an area measure?
options: The variety of alleles within one species
The number of different species present
The number of individuals of one species
The total mass of all organisms present
questions.explanation: Species richness is a simple count of how many species are present. It does not show how many individuals of each species there are.

questions.stem: A region contains coral reefs, mangrove forests, seagrass meadows and sandy islands. Which level of biodiversity does this variety best describe?
options: Ecosystem diversity
Genetic diversity
Species diversity
Population diversity
questions.explanation: A range of different habitats and communities in one region is ecosystem diversity. Species diversity would be the variety of species living in them.

questions.stem: A bushland reserve was surveyed in 1995 and again in 2025. Why is it important that both surveys used the same classification and identification methods?
options: So the reserve's species stay the same from one survey to the next
So every species in the reserve is counted only in the second survey
So the surveys need not record any abiotic factors at either time
So differences in species counts reflect real change, not changes in naming
questions.explanation: Measures of biodiversity rely on consistent classification, so comparisons across time are valid only if species are identified the same way. Otherwise a change in counts might reflect renamed or split species rather than real change.

questions.stem: Which list gives the levels of classification from broadest to narrowest?
options: Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom, domain
Domain, phylum, kingdom, order, class, genus, family, species
Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, domain, class, phylum, family, order, species, genus
questions.explanation: Classification is hierarchical: each level contains one or more groups from the level below it, from the broad domain to the single species. Listing from species upwards reverses the order asked for.

questions.stem: Two animals belong to the same order but to different families. Which level must they also share?
options: Species
Class
Family
Genus
questions.explanation: Organisms in the same order must also share every broader level: class, phylum, kingdom and domain. Being in different families means they cannot share a genus or species.

questions.stem: Jarrah's scientific name is Eucalyptus marginata. Which statement about how such a name is written is correct?
options: The genus has a capital letter; the species name is in lower case
Both words have capitals, because both are proper names
The species name comes first and the genus name second
Only the genus name is written in italics or underlined
questions.explanation: In binomial nomenclature the genus comes first with a capital letter and the species name follows in lower case, and both words are italicised or underlined. The species name is never capitalised.

questions.stem: Species A and B are in the same order but different families. Species A and C are in the same family but different genera. Which pair is most closely related?
options: A and C
A and B
B and C
All three equally
questions.explanation: A and C share a family, a narrower group than the order shared by A and B, so they have a more recent common ancestor. B and C are in different families, so they are related only at the level of order.

questions.stem: A newly described animal has fur, feeds its young on milk and lays eggs. In which group of mammals would it be classified?
options: Placental mammals
Reptiles
Monotremes
Marsupials
questions.explanation: Fur and milk make it a mammal, and laying eggs is the reproductive feature of monotremes, like the platypus and echidnas. Reptiles lay eggs but do not have fur or produce milk.

questions.stem: The Australian marsupial mole and the golden moles of Africa look very alike, but DNA and their reproduction place them in different groups of mammals. Why does classification follow this evidence rather than appearance?
options: DNA changes to match an animal's appearance as it grows
Animals that look alike are always members of one species
Similar features can evolve separately in similar habitats
Appearance is never inherited, so it cannot be used at all
questions.explanation: Burrowing in similar habitats selected for similar body shapes in unrelated lineages, an example of convergent evolution. Molecular sequences and reproduction better reflect evolutionary relatedness than appearance does.

questions.stem: In the scientific name Eucalyptus marginata, what does Eucalyptus refer to?
options: The species
The family
The order
The genus
questions.explanation: The first word of a binomial name is the genus, and the two words together name the species. Many other eucalypts share the genus Eucalyptus.

questions.stem: Mammals are divided into monotremes, marsupials and placental mammals. Which basis of classification does this division mainly use?
options: Type of diet
Habitat they live in
Body size
Method of reproduction
questions.explanation: Monotremes lay eggs, marsupials give birth to tiny young that usually develop in a pouch, and placental mammals nourish the embryo through a placenta. Biological classification uses methods of reproduction along with physical features and molecular sequences.

questions.stem: Archaea and bacteria are both prokaryotes. Why are they placed in separate domains?
options: Archaea are viruses, while bacteria are cells with their own ribosomes
Their molecular sequences, such as ribosomal RNA, differ fundamentally
Archaea have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles but bacteria do not
Archaea are multicellular, while bacteria always live as single cells
questions.explanation: Comparisons of molecular sequences, especially ribosomal RNA, showed archaea are as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes, leading to the three-domain system. Archaea lack a nucleus, like bacteria.

questions.stem: Why does a modern biological classification reflect evolutionary relationships?
options: Groups are based only on where organisms live and what they eat
Organisms are grouped by size, from the largest to the smallest
Organisms are grouped by the date on which they were first named
Groups are based on shared features and sequences inherited from common ancestors
questions.explanation: Shared physical features and similar molecular sequences are largely inherited from common ancestors, so organisms grouped together tend to be closely related. Habitat or diet can be similar in unrelated organisms.

questions.stem: Which pair of organisms is likely to be most closely related?
options: Two species in the same order
Two species in the same phylum
Two species in the same genus
Two species in the same family
questions.explanation: The narrower the shared group, the more recent the common ancestor. A genus is narrower than a family, order or phylum.

questions.stem: DNA evidence shows that a species placed in genus X shares a more recent common ancestor with the species of genus Y. What is most likely to happen to its classification?
options: It becomes a new kingdom, because DNA has overruled its physical features
It may be moved to genus Y once scientists debate and accept the evidence
It must stay in genus X, because a scientific name can never be changed
It is removed from all classification until a fossil confirms the result
questions.explanation: Classification systems follow international conventions and change through debate and resolution as new evidence emerges. Names can be revised to reflect relationships revealed by molecular data.

questions.stem: Why are scientific names governed by international codes of nomenclature?
options: So each species is given a new name in every country it lives in
So common names can replace scientific names in reports
So that a name, once given, can never be revised or debated
So each species has one name used by scientists everywhere
questions.explanation: International conventions give every species a single accepted scientific name, avoiding the confusion of different common names. The codes also set out how names may be changed when evidence warrants it.

questions.stem: Which statement gives a common definition of a species?
options: Organisms that look identical in size, colour and overall body shape
Organisms that can interbreed in natural conditions to produce fertile offspring
Organisms that live in the same habitat and share the same food sources
Organisms that can mate and produce any offspring, fertile or not
questions.explanation: The ability to interbreed and produce fertile offspring under natural conditions is a widely used definition of a species. Producing infertile offspring, as a horse and donkey do, does not meet it.

questions.stem: A horse and a donkey can mate to produce a mule, but mules are infertile. What does this show?
options: Mules are the common ancestor of both
Horses and donkeys are separate species
Horses and donkeys are the same species
Mules are a new species of their own
questions.explanation: Because the offspring are infertile, horses and donkeys do not meet the interbreeding definition of a single species. A mule cannot found a population, so it is not a new species.

questions.stem: Why can the interbreeding definition of a species not be applied to bacteria?
options: They all belong to a single species, so no definition is needed
They interbreed with every other bacterium, whatever its species
They reproduce asexually by binary fission, without interbreeding
They are too small to be seen, so their offspring cannot be counted
questions.explanation: Bacteria reproduce asexually, so the test of producing fertile offspring by interbreeding does not apply; they are grouped by genetic and structural similarity instead. This is one of the exceptions every species definition meets.

questions.stem: Two frog populations look identical, but their DNA differs greatly, their calls differ, and they do not interbreed where they meet. What do these findings show?
options: They are one species, because frogs that look alike must share all alleles
They are hybrids, because two species that interbreed always look the same
They are separate species, so a definition based on appearance alone fails
They are one species, because physical similarity outweighs DNA evidence
questions.explanation: Genetic difference and the lack of interbreeding show they are separate species that happen to look alike. Such cryptic species are an exception to definitions based on morphological similarity.

questions.stem: The males and females of a bird species look so different that early naturalists described them as two species. Which kind of species definition misled them?
options: One based on similarity of DNA sequences
One based on the order of their amino acids
One based on physical (morphological) similarity
One based on the ability to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: Large differences in appearance between the sexes (sexual dimorphism) make a definition based on appearance unreliable. Observing that the two forms interbreed, or comparing their DNA, shows they are one species.

questions.stem: Why can the interbreeding definition not be used to decide whether two fossil specimens belong to the same species?
options: Fossil organisms were all asexual, so they never needed to interbreed
Fossils of the same species always occur in the same rock layer
The organisms are extinct, so their ability to breed cannot be tested
Fossils contain no physical features that can be measured or compared
questions.explanation: Extinct organisms cannot be tested for producing fertile offspring, so palaeontologists rely on physical features, and sometimes ancient DNA, to define fossil species. Fossils often preserve many measurable features.

questions.stem: Two eucalypt species growing where their ranges overlap sometimes produce fertile hybrids. What does this show about species definitions?
options: Plants never interbreed, so the hybrids must be caused by mutation
Species recognised by other evidence can still sometimes interbreed
The two eucalypts must really be one species with two different names
The hybrids are infertile, so the definition is not affected at all
questions.explanation: Fertile hybrids between otherwise distinct species occur in many plants, including eucalypts. This is an exception to the interbreeding definition, which is why biologists use several lines of evidence.

questions.stem: What is a dichotomous key?
options: A list of every species found in an area, arranged in alphabetical order
A diagram showing the feeding relationships between species in a habitat
A tree that shows the evolutionary history of a group using DNA data
An identification tool in which each step offers two contrasting choices
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key leads to an identification through a series of paired, contrasting statements. Feeding relationships are shown in food webs, and evolutionary history in phylogenetic trees.

questions.stem: Key: 1a Six legs, go to 2; 1b Eight legs, spider. 2a Wings present, go to 3; 2b No wings, silverfish. 3a Hard front wings cover the back wings, beetle; 3b Two pairs of clear wings, wasp. An animal has six legs and two pairs of clear wings. What is it?
options: Spider
Wasp
Beetle
Silverfish
questions.explanation: Six legs leads to step 2, wings present leads to step 3, and two pairs of clear wings identifies a wasp. A beetle's hard front wings would cover its back wings.

questions.stem: Using the same key (1a six legs, 1b eight legs; 2a wings, 2b no wings; 3a hard front wings, 3b two pairs of clear wings), which single observation separates a silverfish from a beetle?
options: Whether the wings are clear
Whether wings are present
The number of legs
Whether the front wings are hard
questions.explanation: Both have six legs, so they part at step 2: the beetle has wings and the silverfish has none. The type of wings is only compared at step 3, after the silverfish has already been identified.

questions.stem: Which feature is most suitable for a step in a dichotomous key?
options: The number of legs on the animal
Whether the animal is larger than most
Whether the animal is common in the area
How active the animal seems today
questions.explanation: Good key features are clear, observable and do not change, such as the number of legs. Relative size, abundance or behaviour on one day are subjective or variable.

questions.stem: A rocky shore and a sandy beach in the same climate support very different communities. Which abiotic factor best explains this difference?
options: Temperature
Day length
Substrate
Rainfall
questions.explanation: Substrate is the surface or material organisms live on or in, such as rock or sand, and it determines which organisms can attach, burrow or feed. The shores share the same climate, so rainfall, temperature and day length are similar.

questions.stem: Large-scale environments such as deserts, tropical rainforests and temperate grasslands are classified mainly by which abiotic factor?
options: The age of the rocks below the soil
The species of the dominant predator
Climate, especially temperature and rainfall
The number of animal species present
questions.explanation: Climate largely determines the type of vegetation an area supports, so it is used to describe and classify major environments. Species counts and predators are biotic features, not abiotic ones.

questions.stem: Which is an example of collaboration within a species?
options: A python catching and eating a native rat in the bush
Two plant species competing for light in a forest gap
Ants of one colony working together to forage and defend the nest
A tick feeding on the blood of a kangaroo without killing it
questions.explanation: Collaboration is cooperation between members of the same species that benefits the group. The other examples are parasitism, predation and competition between species.

questions.stem: A disease sharply reduces the number of a small native mammal that a predator eats and that competes with another herbivore. What is the most likely result?
options: The competing herbivore will decline because it caught the disease
No other species will change, because disease affects one host
Predator numbers may fall and the competing herbivore may increase
Predator numbers will rise because the prey is easier to catch
questions.explanation: Disease is an interaction that can reduce a host population, and the effect spreads through the community: predators lose food and competitors gain resources. Effects rarely stay confined to one species.
